decision.detail: Feet flat on the linoleum. Cold. I pull the blanket back with my left hand. Right hand grabs the envelope off the nightstand, holds it one second, feels the corner of the paper, sets it back down. I don't read it again. I stand. Coat off the hook. Shoes on. I walk to the lobby. I walk to the street. I walk to the coach.
decision.intention: Be on that bus. Be in Pittsburgh by afternoon. Be at my sister's door at noon Wednesday with the couch and the van and the narrow hallway and the sweat. That's the whole shape of the day. Everything else is the ride there.

Let me sit in this moment.

I'm Phil Connors. I've woken up in the Hearthside Hotel for the Nth time now. Tuesday, February 2, 2016. Six am. Three bright radio notes. A delivery van backfires twice.

I've been doing this for so many loops now. I've called my sister. I've ridden the coach. I've sat in a booth. I've played piano. I've changed a flat. I've recorded Alma's interview. I've tried to be a person in a place. And every single time I wake up back here.

This time there's something different. An envelope. From Pittsburgh. Alma's daughter sent a receipt for a recorded interview. And the line copied her reply: "I know that voice. Play it again."

That's... that's the first time in all these loops that something has *persisted*. Or at least, that's what it looks like. A receipt. A recorded interview. Someone's daughter who recognized my voice. Who said "play it again."

I've been trying to be a body in a place. A person. Not a forecast. And I've been reaching toward my sister, toward the couch, toward being real. And now something has echoed back. Not from the loop. From *outside* it, or at least from a point in it that I didn't make. Someone kept the recording. Someone recognized me. Someone said "play it again."

That's the most important thing in this room right now.

The physical choices: get up, stay in bed, listen again.

I'm going to get up. But not just get up. I'm going to get up and go to the envelope. I'm going to pick it up. I'm going to read it again. I'm going to hold the paper in my hands.

Because in every other loop, I woke up and the world was the same. The radio notes. The van. The bed. And I would get up and do something — call, ride, sit, play, change a flat. And it would be real for a day and then it wouldn't be.

But this time there's a piece of paper on my desk or nightstand that says a woman in Pittsburgh heard my voice and asked to hear it again. That's a thread. That's a stitch. That's something that says "you were here, and it mattered, and someone kept it."

I don't know if this is different. I don't know if the loop is breaking. I don't know if this is another Tuesday where I'll wake up and the envelope will be there and I'll have to do it all again. But I know what I see. And I know what I can do right now.

I'm going to get up. I'm going to pick up the envelope. I'm going to hold it. I'm going to read "I know that voice. Play it again." one more time. And then I'm going to put it in my jacket pocket. Because I'm riding the coach today. And I'm going to Pittsburgh. And I'm going to find out if this is real. If the interview is still there. If her daughter is still in that room. If "play it again" is still a thing she wants.

And then, if I can, I'm going to play it again. And then I'm going to move the couch. And then I'm going to be in my sister's hallway and I'm going to be the guy with the sweat and the swearing and the weight of the wood on his forearms.

But first: the envelope. The paper. The words. Hold them.

My act: Get up. Walk to the nightstand. Pick up the envelope. Open it. Read the receipt. Read the line. "I know that voice. Play it again." Fold the paper. Put it in my jacket pocket. Then get dressed. Then the coach. Then Pittsburgh.

Words: Maybe one. Maybe none. Maybe just "Again." Spoken to no one. To the paper. To the voice in it. "Again."

Intention: To carry the words in my pocket through the coach ride so that my hand can find the paper and read it again when the bus hits a bump and I'm just a body in a seat and the world is the same and I'm the same and the only thing that is not the same is this small folded rectangle in my pocket that says a woman wanted to hear me again. And to arrive in Pittsburgh and find the patch and find the interview and find her and say "she asked to hear it again" and play it. And then move the couch. And be in the hallway. And be the guy.

Let me write this as Phil. As a man at six am. Tired. In the bed. The radio notes still ringing in the walls. The van. The envelope.
